Overview


I am a Master of Public Health candidate at Morehouse School of Medicine with experience across community health, research, data analysis, healthcare, and organizational operations. My current work centers on understanding how people experience health systems, identifying gaps in access and service delivery, and translating data and community perspectives into practical solutions. I am especially interested in chronic disease prevention, social and structural influences on health, community-informed intervention design, and the use of data to support better public health decision-making.

title: The story behind the work.
text:
MY PHILOSOPHY


More than a number. The numbers only matter because the people do.






ABOUT ME


The story behind the work.

My path into public health has never followed a single straight line. With a foundation in chemistry and experiences spanning clinical care, lab research, data, business, marketing and communication, and community health, I have learned to approach health from multiple perspectives. Each experience has strengthened my curiosity about the patterns behind health outcomes—not only what is happening, but why it is happening, who is affected, and where meaningful change can occur.


That curiosity ultimately led me to epidemiology, where I found a way to connect my analytical nature with my commitment to people. I am especially interested in using data to understand disease burden, healthcare access, and the conditions that shape opportunities for prevention. Whether I am analyzing a dataset, developing a visualization, working within a community, or solving an operational problem, I am most energized by work that transforms information into something useful for the people behind the numbers.









PUBLIC HEALTH • PURPOSE • DIRECTION


My work sits at the intersection of epidemiology, chronic disease prevention, healthcare, and community health. As I continue developing as a public health professional and researcher, my goal is to bridge evidence with action—using data to ask better questions, design practical solutions, and contribute to systems of care that strengthen prevention and improve health within communities.

title: Lab 7: Interactive Plotly Visualization
text:
Build Interactive Trend Graph

#|label: trend-graph

interactive_trend <- ggplot(
  continent_trends,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = mean_life_expectancy,
    color = continent,
    text = paste0(
      "<b>",
      continent,
      "</b>",
      "<br>Year: ",
      year,
      "<br>Mean life expectancy: ",
      round(
        mean_life_expectancy,
        digits = 1
      ),
      " years"
    )
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Life Expectancy Increased Across Continents",
    subtitle = "Hover over a point or zoom into time period",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean life expectancy in years",
    color = "Continent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 13
  )

) %>%

    hoverinfo = "skip",
    traces = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9)
  ) %>%
  layout(
    hovermode = "x unified"
  ) %>%
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text: The purpose of this project is to demonstrate the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to visualize and interpret county-level public health data. Using Georgia counties and simulated vaccination coverage data, this project explores different mapping techniques to identify geographic patterns and communicate public health information. Static and interactive maps were developed to demonstrate how geographic data can support public health analysis and decision-making.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Setup

#|label: load-packages

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(maps)
library(leaflet)
library(htmltools)

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Georgia County Boundaries

#|label: county-boundaries

georgia_counties <- maps::map(
  database = "county",
  regions = "georgia",
  plot = FALSE,
  fill = TRUE
) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  rename(
    county_id = ID
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    county_name = str_remove(
      county_id,
      "^georgia,"
    ),
    county_name = str_to_title(
      county_name
    )
  )

georgia_counties <- st_make_valid(georgia_counties)


#|label: georgia-county-map

ggplot(
  data = georgia_counties
) +
  geom_sf(
    fill = "#F3F4F6",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Georgia County Boundaries",
    subtitle = "Each polygon can be joined to county-level health information",
    caption = "Boundary data: maps R package"
  ) +
  theme_void()

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Simulated Health Data

#|label: health-data

set.seed(716)

county_health <- georgia_counties %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  distinct(
    county_id,
    county_name
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    vaccination_rate = pmin(
      pmax(
        rnorm(
          n = n (),
          mean = 71,
          sd = 6
        ),
        45
      ),
      95
    ),
    child_population = round(
      runif(
        n = n (),
        min = 1500,
        max = 75000
      )
    ),
    target_status = if_else(
      vaccination_rate >= 80,
      "Met Target",
      "Below Target"
    )
  )

county_health %>%
  select(
    county_name,
    vaccination_rate,
    child_population,
    target_status
  ) %>%
  slice_head(
    n = 8
  )

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Continuous Choropleth

#|label: continuous-map

ggplot(
  data = county_map_data
) +
  geom_sf(
    mapping = aes(
      fill = vaccination_rate
    ),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    direction = 1,
    limits = c(
      45,
      95
    ),
    name = "Vaccination\ncoverage (%)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Simulated Vaccination Coverage Varied Across Georgia Counties",
    subtitle = "Example data created for instructional purposes",
    caption = "Boundary data: maps R package | Health values are simulated"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )














NoteMap Interpretation



This map illustrates variation in simulated vaccination coverage across Georgia counties using a continuous color scale. Differences in color intensity allow viewers to identify geographic patterns in vaccination rates.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Classified Choropleth

#|label: county-classification

county_map_data <- county_map_data %>%
  mutate(
    coverage_status = case_when(
      vaccination_rate < 70 ~ "Below 70%",
      vaccination_rate < 80 ~ "70% to 79.9%",
      vaccination_rate >= 80 ~ "80% or higher",
      TRUE ~ "Missing"
    ),
    coverage_status = factor(
      coverage_status,
      levels = c(
        "Below 70%",
        "70% to 79.9%",
        "80% or higher",
        "Missing"
      )
    )
  )


#|label: classified-map

ggplot(
  data = county_map_data
) +
  geom_sf(
    mapping = aes(
      fill = coverage_status
    ),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Below 70%" = "#D55E00",
      "70% to 79.9%" = "#E69F00",
      "80% or higher" = "#355E3B"
    ),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Counties Below the Example Target Are Easy to Identify",
    subtitle = "Categories are based on instructional thresholds",
    caption = "Boundary data: maps R package | Health values are simulated"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )














NoteMap Interpretation



This map categorizes simulated county-level vaccination coverage into three groups based on example thresholds of Below 70%, 70% to 79.9%, and 80% or higher. This classification allows viewers to distinguish counties with lower vaccination coverage from those meeting or exceeding the 80% target.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Point Map

#|label: clinic-points

set.seed(718)

clinic_points <- county_map_data %>%
  slice_sample(
    n = 20
  ) %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  transmute(
    clinic_name = paste(
      county_name,
      "Community Clinic"
    ),
    annual_visits = round(
      runif(
        n = n(),
        min = 500,
        max = 12000
      )
    )
  )


#|label: point-map

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = georgia_counties,
    fill = "grey95",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = clinic_points,
    size = 2.5,
    color = "#0072B2"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Simulated Community Clinic Locations",
    subtitle = "Points are generated for instructional purposes",
    caption = "Boundary data: maps R package | Clinic locations are simulated"
  ) +
  theme_void()














NoteMap Interpretation



This map displays simulated geographic locations of 20 community clinics across Georgia counties. The points are used to illustrate and represent how healthcare facilities are spatially distributed, but do not indicate actual clinic locations or available services.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Proportional-Symbol Map

#|label: proportional-symbol-map

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = georgia_counties,
    fill = "grey95",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = clinic_points,
    mapping = aes(
      size = annual_visits
    ),
    color = "#0072B2",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  scale_size_area(
    max_size = 11,
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    name = "Annual visits"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Simulated Clinic Volume Varied Across Locations",
    subtitle = "Symbol area represents annual visits",
    caption = "Boundary data: maps R package | Clinic locations and visits are simulated"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right"
  )














NoteMap Interpretation



This map displays simulated community clinic locations with proportional symbols based on annual clinic visits. Differences in symbol size allow viewers to compare simulated service utilization across clinic locations.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Interactive Leaflet Map

#|label: leaflet-map

county_leaflet <- county_map_data %>%
  st_transform(
    crs = 4326
  )

coverage_palette <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = county_leaflet$vaccination_rate,
  na.color = "#BDBDBD"
)

county_labels <- paste0(
  "<strong>",
  htmlEscape(
    county_leaflet$county_name
  ),
  " County</strong>",
  "<br>Simulated vaccination coverage: ",
  round(
    county_leaflet$vaccination_rate,
    digits = 1
  ),
  "%",
  "<br>Simulated child population: ",
  scales::comma(
    county_leaflet$child_population
  )
) %>%
  lapply(
    HTML
  )


leaflet(
  data = county_leaflet,
  options = leafletOptions(
    minZoom = 5
  )
) %>%
  addProviderTiles(
    providers$CartoDB.Positron
  ) %>%
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~coverage_palette(
      vaccination_rate
    ),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.6,
    opacity = 1,
    label = county_labels,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      weight = 2,
      color = "#333333",
      fillOpacity = 0.9,
      bringToFront = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    pal = coverage_palette,
    values = ~vaccination_rate,
    title = "Simulated coverage (%)",
    position = "bottomright",
    opacity = 0.8

NoteMap Interpretation



This interactive map allows viewers to explore simulated vaccination coverage across Georgia counties. County-level labels provide additional information on vaccination rates and child population, supporting geographic comparisons.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Limitations
There are several limitations to accurately interpreting GIS mapping and spatial analysis. In this project, most of the data including vaccination rates, child population, clinic locations, and annual visit counts were simulated for instructional purposes and do not represent actual public health information for the state of Georgia. Additionally, county-level data may inaccurately depict variations within individual communities and should not be used to make assumptions about individual health behaviors. The third limitation to consider is that simulated clinic locations were generated using county centroids, which may not accurately represent the geographic distributions of healthcare facilities and accessibility of services.

title: GIS Mapping for Public Health
text:
Ethical and Accessibility Considerations
Ethical and accessibility considerations are important to ensure public health information is interpreted and communicated appropriately. Public health professionals should also be cautious about generalizing geographic patterns or stigmatizing counties based on differences in vaccination rates or health demographics. Additionally, the inclusion of exact locations of health-related facilities should be carefully considered to address potential privacy or safety concerns. Missing data and uncertainty should be clearly communicated to promote transparency and prevent misleading interpretations. Maps should include clear titles, subtitles, captions, legends, and data source information to support accurate interpretation. Accessible color schemes should also be considered to improve visibility. Static maps or data tables should be available as alternatives for individuals who may have difficulty using or understanding interactive maps.
